thread.title: Sensei Positions For 2019: What You Should Expect Next Year

author: Dividend Sensei
title: Sensei Positions For 2019: What You Should Expect Next Year
text:
(Source: imgflip )
After a blissful 2017 when the market rose 22% with a peak drawdown (from all-time highs) of 3%, 2018 has seen volatility come roaring back with a vengeance. Today, the stock market ( SPY ) ( DIA ) ( QQQ ) is experiencing its second correction of the year, something that has only occurred three times since 1965 (1971, 2015, 2018).
SPY Total Return Price data by YCharts
As a result, stocks have, after a year of high drama, rewarded investors with flat returns. In fact, the S&P 500 is now slightly negative for the year and threatening to break a nine-year winning streak that is tied for the longest in US history, matching the epic bull market of the 1990s.
(Source: Ben Carlson, Wealth Of Common Sense)
While investors are eager to put 2018 in the rearview mirror, the biggest question most of us have is "what's 2019 going to look like". So let's take a look at what factors are likely to drive the market next year, what that means for your portfolio, as well as how I'm positioning my own retirement portfolio to thrive in the long-term no matter what 2019 might bring.
What do you expect to be the key driver of stock market performance in 2019? I'm a stock-focused investor/analyst and expect four key things will likely to be the biggest drivers for next year. Just like this year, they include
Fed rate policy Trade war risk US economic/yield curve risk Slowing Global economy While I'll discuss all of these issues in detail in a moment it's important that investors remember that the volatility we're seeing this year is likely to continue for two main reasons. As Blackstone's ( BX ) Byron Wien explains:
Recent research suggests that 60%-90% of daily equity trading is now performed by algorithmic trading, up from 25% in 2004 . Meanwhile, passive exchange-traded funds have directed trillions of dollars into equity markets since 2009, and the percent of the U.S. equity market share captured by passive strategies has increased from 26% at the start of 2009 to 47% as of 3Q'18. All of these trends are likely to increase volatility moving forward ." Byron Wien (emphasis added)
During turbulent and scary times like these retail investors are playing a dominant role due to panic selling. For example, according to analyst firm Lipper from December 5th to December 12th investors pulled a record $46 billion out of US stock ETFs (and a near-record $13 billion from bond ETFs) and poured $81 billion into money market accounts. With nearly half of US stocks now owned by ETFs, blind investor panic selling is going to cause bigger swings in the largest and most popularly owned names that make up the largest weighting in each index, like Apple ( AAPL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), and Amazon ( AMZN ).
What's more, with about 75% of daily trading now run by computerized algorithms we can expect to see sharp volatility in the future as well. That's for two reasons. First many algos are programmed to sell when certain technical indicators occur (such as a death cross or an index falling below its 200-day moving average). In addition, more algos are now scanning headlines, including social media like Twitter ( TWTR ) and trading instantly based on keywords pertaining to all the risk factors the market is currently fixated on. In the era of "fake news" and Trump tweeting frequently (and often off the cuff), these algos can create massive intraday market swings of 3% like we've seen during this correction. It also means the risks of a flash crash are higher, though those are usually short, intraday events (though tough to stomach when investor's nerves are this raw).
As we approach 2019, are you bullish or bearish on U.S. stocks/your preferred asset class? Like Warren Buffett, I'm always a long-term bull on US stocks. That's because they have proven to be the best performing asset class in history.
(Source: Credit Suisse)
And given my unique risk profile (I'm 32 years, self-employed with six sources of income, and a 90% post-tax savings rate) I can afford to have 100% of my life savings in stocks at all times. But keep in mind that I've been investing since the age of nine (started two years younger than Buffett) and have personally invested through three 50+% market/industry crashes
Tech bubble Financial Crisis The Great Oil Crash of 2014-2016 (crude plunged 76% and I was buying quality midstream stocks the entire time) I'm more than comfortable with extreme volatility and buying stocks (if I have cash) or holding quality names (if I don't) even for multi-year periods of falling prices.
Your personal asset allocation (mix of cash/bonds/stocks) should be based on your individual circumstances and goals (talk with a certified fiduciary financial advisor to determine what that is).
(Source: Morningstar)
The reason that I embrace volatility like a lover, is because I know that the market's incredible wealth compounding power isn't despite volatility, but precisely because of it. It may surprise readers to learn that if you missed just 50 of the best single market days over the past 20 years (less than 0.01% of all trading days), your total returns would have fallen from 7.2% CAGR to -4.5% (a 60% portfolio decline). This shows the dangers of market timing and trying to avoid the market's biggest losses, which happen to cluster with its strongest gains.
(Source: Morningstar)
Since I'm focused on getting rich over time, I focus on the long-term statistics which show that stocks go up in 74% of years. And over longer time periods, the probability of making money rises to 86% (over five years) and 100% over 15 years. Note that even investors who bought at the market top in 1929, before stocks crashed 90% at one point during The Great Depression, were still sitting on positive returns by 1944 (and pretty nice ones too).
Ultimately stock prices are a function of the fundamentals, meaning earnings, cash flow, and dividends. As long as the economy grows over time and those fundamentals rise, stock prices will also climb steadily higher over the long-term.
But as far as any given year goes? Well, while predicting the market's returns in any given year is an educated guesstimate at best, here's why I expect the S&P 500 to deliver 0% to 10% total returns next year.
Which domestic/global issue is most likely to adversely affect U.S. markets in the coming year? If the Fed isn't dovish enough then the markets will be unhappy in 2019. The current dot plot shows five or six (even split) more rate hikes this tightening cycle. But the bond market is pricing in far fewer hikes due to declining growth and inflation expectations.
According to Bloomberg, short-term (two-year) inflation expectations have fallen recently to 1.2% (for Consumer Price Index) while long-term (10 and 30-year) expectations are now below the Fed's 2.0% long-term target. Keep in mind the Fed is officially looking at core PCE, which generally runs slightly lower than CPE. This is why the Bond market is now expecting just two rate hikes in total and even the Fed to start cutting rates in 2020.
At the December 19th meeting, the Fed's guidance (dot plot) and its statement might not match the bond market's more pessimistic economic outlook. For example, if the Fed telegraphs two more rate hikes for 2019 (so a total of three more), then I'd expect the market to react negatively. Personally, given the current inflation fundamentals (core PCE is at 1.8% and falling from a peak of 2.0% this year) I agree with St. Louis Fed President James Bullard that the Fed should not hike in December (there is any need too). Bullard will be a voting FOMC member in 2019, but a rate hike on December 19th is very likely to happen.
Trade is the other major wildcard for next year. Friday, December 12th the market fell 1.9% when weak economic news from China stoked fears that its economic growth will come in far lower than expected next year.
(Source: Bloomberg)
China's manufacturing sector is now on the verge of contracting and is showing the weakest growth since June 2016. The US tariffs already imposed are merely compounding the negative factors that have been weakening China's growth for years (workforce has been shrinking since 2014). That is likely why China is now making strong overtures on trade including
postpones higher tariffs on $126 billion in US imports scheduled to go into effect January 1st buying as much as 3 million tons of US corn as early as January Lowering tariffs on US cars from 40% to 15% (a retaliatory tariff imposed in July) But it's important to remember that economists think that 90 days is too short to achieve a final trade deal with China. The issues we're negotiating are highly complex and so these moves by Beijing are merely designed to extend the March 1st deadline in order to avoid US tariffs on 50% of China's imports rising from their current effective rate of 12.5% to 25%. They are also designed to avoid Trump's threat of up to 25% tariffs on $267 billion of additional imports (the other half of US/China imports).
While negotiations are ongoing the current US tariffs are likely to remain in effect. How long might negotiations last? Well given the complexity of the issues involved (including China's IP theft against US companies) it might potentially take as long as the US/Canada/Mexico NAFTA renegotiations. While ultimately the new USMCA agreement was finalized, those negotiations began in May 2017 and didn't conclude until September 2018 . That 15 month period has me thinking that, given the slowing of the US/China and global economy, negotiations are likely to take six to 12 months, since that both sides are feeling immense pressures to eliminate the growth headwinds created by tariffs.
(Source: Bloomberg) - above 50 indicates positive growth
The global economy, while not likely to fall into recession, is feeling the effects of the trade conflict (one of several factors slowing growth). Eliminating this overhang is important but investors need to be prepared for trade uncertainty (and wild headline-driven volatility) to continue through the first half of 2019 at least, and possibly through the end of the year.
In a worst-case scenario, the animosity trade hawks in the Trump administration (like Navarro and Trump himself) feel towards China might even drag this out for as long as 18 months (deal struck mid-2020). The good news is that I'm highly confident that a deal will ultimately get done, if only because the slowing US economy would be hurt even more by the US imposing 25% tariffs on all Chinese imports.
(Source: New York Federal Reserve)
The New York Fed is now estimating that, based on the latest leading economic indicator reports, the US economy is growing at 2.4% in Q4, and is likely to continue that much weaker growth rate in Q1. Note that in Q2 and Q3 we grew at 4.2% and 3.5%, respectively. 2.4% growth isn't terrible, but it is below the 2.5% the Fed was expecting in 2019, as well as the 2.5% and 2.7% the IMF and OECD are currently forecasting.
(Source: Forexlive ) - November estimates
You'll note that the OECD isn't expecting any major economy or the world economy to fall into a recession anytime soon. But growth is slowing and a trade war is merely throwing sand into the economic gears that need to be eliminated if the market is finally to breathe a sigh of relief (and likely end this correction by hitting new all-time highs).
How does the political climate affect the risks and opportunities for next year? Historically basing investing decisions on short-term news in general, but political expectations, in particular, is a terrible idea. None other than Warren Buffet, the greatest investor in history things that " if you mix politics and investing you're making a big mistake. "
But that doesn't mean that investors still don't let short-term news affect long-term decisions. According to an August Raymond James survey of 1,000 US investors with at least $75,000 in the markets in August, 40% said that politics were either "extremely or very important." Worst still, 70% said that news headlines in general influence their investment decisions .
This is likely to end up hurting the average investor, who over the past 20 years, thanks to such attempts at market timing, has managed to drastically underperform literally every single asset class.
As Simona Mocuta, a senior economist with State Street Global Advisors explains,
Policy risk is becoming more of the issue. It is overshadowing the good macro story ...There has been a shift in perception. People are ignoring good fundamentals because the political noise is bad. " - Simona Mocuta, (emphasis added)
The key to good long-term investing is ALWAYS to think of your portfolio as a business. It's literally a holding company that owns partial stakes in other companies. So the things to focus on are the fundamentals, both at the company level, and at the macroeconomic level.
That's opposed to making short-term and emotionally driven decisions based on fear and headlines.
I have a gut and my gut tells me more sometimes than anybody else's brain can ever tell me. " - President Trump
(Source: CNBC )
Despite what our President and many investors may believe, the stock market is NOT a good indicator of economic health or able to predict recessions with accuracy. This is why I totally ignore short-term stock prices and instead focus on what I like to call the "3 Bs".
big macro ( weekly analysis of over 19 leading economic indicators, seen through seven economic models/meta-analyses I trust) bond yields: 10y-3m yield curve is the most accurate recession predictor ever discovered Buffett: I track Berkshire's ( BRK.B ) 13-F each quarter to see how much and what Buffett is buying. Berkshire has its finger in every part of the US economy and if Buffett is aggressively buying stocks (as he did in Q3 to the tune of $12.6 billion in net purchases near the market's all-time high) it likely means Berkshire doesn't expect a recession anytime soon.
(Source: Barron's)
That's especially true if Buffett is buying massive amounts of economically sensitive stocks like $13.3 billion worth of banks. Basically, the 3Bs will give investors a much better idea of the state of the economy and provide far better recession warning than tracking the market's manic short-term swings or the financial media's hysterical headlines.
Speaking of bond markets, let's discuss the yield curve, which the media has been obsessing over recently. While that's for good reason, long-term investors need to separate fact from fiction about the best recession predictor in history.
Do you expect the yield curve to continue flattening in 2019, and if so what impacts will that have on the equity market and the economy in general? It seems these days we're all watching the yield curve, the difference between bond yields on different duration Treasury bonds. That's understandable given that according to a March 2018 report from the San Francisco Fed, an inverted yield curve has " correctly signaled all nine recessions since 1955 and had only one false positive, in the mid-1960s, when an inversion was followed by an economic slowdown but not an official recession."
But it's important to realize that there are dozens of yield curves and according to an August 2018 study by the San Francisco Fed, " The best summary measure is the spread between the ten-year and three-month yields. " While the 10y-2y curve is the most famous and what the market is more focused on, according to an October Dallas Fed bank survey the 10y-3m (most accurate curve) is what banks are focused on.
Banks were also asked how their lending policies would potentially change in response to a hypothetical moderate inversion of the (10y-3m) yield curve prevailing over the next year. Significant shares of banks indicated that they would tighten their standards or price terms across every major loan category if the yield curve were to invert ...Those banks that indicated they would tighten their lending policies because of an inversion of the yield curve were asked to provide reasons for their response. Major shares of banks indicated that their bank would interpret this scenario as signaling a less favorable or more uncertain economic outlook and as likely being followed by a deterioration in the quality of their existing loan portfolio . In addition, major shares of banks reported lending would become less profitable and their bank's risk tolerance would decrease in this scenario . " - Dallas Federal Reserve Bank Survey (emphasis added)
So, while the media might be hyping that the 5y-3y warning curve inverted (back on December 3rd, it's not uninverted) investors need to focus on the most accurate yield curve. Here there's both good and bad news.
The bad news is that since April 2010 the 10y-3m yield curve has been steadily flattening. The curve has begun tracking the long-term trend line much closer ever since the Fed began tapering QE (in mid-2013) and then ended it in October 2014. At its current rate of flattening the 10y-3m curve (which is at 0.47% as of December 12th) will invert in 14.5 months (February 2020). The good news is that even when that happens the next recession is likely at least a year away.
My best estimate for when a recession is likely to start (based on the 10y-3m curve flattening) is in 23.5 to 30.5 months (December 2020 to July 2021). That roughly in line with the other macroeconomic data trends and estimates I've seen from Blackstone ( BX ), Bank of America ( BAC ), Deutsche Bank ( DB ), David Rice (over at BaR), and the Fed itself.
But just because the most important yield curve isn't likely to invert soon doesn't mean that the 10y-2y curve won't, or that the market won't freak out over it. In fact, fears of the 10y-2y yield curve inverting might become a self-fulling prophecy. For example, should the Fed's guidance on December 19th signal three more rate hikes are coming, then the two-year yield might spike higher, and market fears of yield curve inversion could send stocks down. That could trigger a flight to safety into 10-year treasuries, lowering that yield curve (0.16% as of December 12th) and flattening it into the single digits.
At which point fear of an inversion could feed on itself and cause more selling, more 10-year bond buying (driving down the 10-year yield) and cause the very inversion that investors worry about.
But guess what? Even if that scenario plays out, and the 10y-2y curve inverts in late 2018 or early 2019, it still means we're about 17 months away from a recession starting.

If the yield curve inverts around January 1st, then the next recession could start in May 2021. And that's only if the 2y-10y yield curve stays inverted. A flight to safety inversion can be short-lived and when fears calm and stocks rise once more the 10-year yield can rise back above the 2-year yield, canceling the recession countdown.
What about the bear market that investors are actually worried about (and why we watch the yield curve to know when a recession is likely coming)? Well, even the 10y-2y inversion typically means that stocks are still 13 to 19 months away from peaking, and the bull market usually has another 22% worth of gains in the tank.
Could this time be different? Sure. Market history is merely a rough, probabilistic guide of what's likely to happen, not a guarantee of what will happen. But the point is that while the yield curve is likely to keep flattening in 2019, and the 10y-2y is likely to invert next year, investors need to know that the 10y-3m curve is the one most worth watching. And even when the 10y-2y finally does invert (no recession clock starts ticking until it's officially negative) there are three important things to keep in mind.
If it rises into positive territory again then the recession clock stops ticking if it stays inverted no recession is likely in 2019 the bull market is still likely to survive for another 13 to 19 months (and stocks are likely to hit new all-time highs). This brings me to the most important thing to discuss, which is how we position our portfolios for 2019.
In terms of asset allocation, how are you positioned heading into the New Year? As I explained earlier I'm 100% in stocks and due to my unique situation and risk profile (and 22 years of market experience), I plan to always be primarily invested in stocks. Now in the event that the 3Bs end up signaling a recession is fast approaching I may start stockpiling some cash (possibly in 2020) to get ready for the bear market bargains we'll see during the next downturn. BUT I must make 100% clear that I am NOT a market timer. I may track the state of the economy and bond yields very closely BUT I WILL NEVER sell 100% of my stocks and go to cash ahead of a coming downturn. That's because all macro analysis is merely probabilistic.
Rather I use my macro analysis to determine what I do with new money. What I own now I plan to keep as long as the investment thesis doesn't break or a stock I own doesn't become wildly overvalued. If it does I will consider selling 50% of it to invest that money into a better opportunity (a more undervalued, higher-yielding and or faster-growing company). Like Buffett, my ideal time horizon for owning a stock is "forever" and as long as the reason I bought a company remains intact, and it doesn't become crazy overvalued (50% or more), then I'll never sell my position entirely.
However, I do want to point out that late cycle corrections like this are actually a blessing for all investors, for two reasons. First, they allow you to buy great companies at fantastic prices (I've invested $100K in 13 companies in this correction and my dry powder is now gone).
More importantly, times of peak fear, uncertainty and doubt like we have today are a great opportunity to perform a "fire drill" on your asset allocation. What I mean is that the S&P 500 is down just 11.3% from its all-time high and thus far stocks have been falling for about three months. Since 1965 the average correction has seen stocks fall 12.3% for three months before bottoming and then climbing back to record highs over four months.
Those figures include this year's two corrections. These past few months that to some have felt like "market hell" has actually been a totally average correction. If you've been losing sleep over an 11.3% downturn? Well, it means your risk tolerance is NOT what you thought it was. Risk tolerances (and thus what asset allocation is right for you) changes over time, as you get older and closer to retirement and or your life circumstances change.
If this correction has shown you that you're too heavy in stocks? Well then when we finally climb out of this correction (which is likely based on the macro earnings and economic fundamentals), you might want to consider selling some stocks and adding to your cash/bond positions. Note I'm not saying to sell now, at what's likely to be near the market bottom. Rather I'm saying that investors should use this correction as a chance to test their emotional and mental discipline against what an actual bear market will feel like.
According to Fisher Investments, the typical bear market isn't a continuous and violent slide downward (i.e. a very long version of what we've seen in the past three months). Rather it's a gradual drift lower for stocks (usually about 12 months) and then the final third of the bear market (six months coinciding with actual negative economic growth) sees the kind of high volatility and sharp daily drops we're seeing now.
In fact, here's what Fisher says about the difference between a bear market and a correction .
Bear markets usually start gradually, lulling investors into complacency. Often investors are still euphoric , having enjoyed years of strong returns, and choose to dismiss warning signs like an inverted 10-year minus 3-month Treasury yield curve or a negative trend in The Conference Board's Leading Economic Indexes. Euphoria can be blinding. The gentle early declines don't seem scary, creating a false sense of security. Deep pessimism typically doesn't arrive until the bear market's darkest days, which usually come in its final one-third or so . By then, it is usually too late for investors to do anything about, lest they risk missing the rebound. But when a correction strikes, sentiment usually darkens quickly. Sometimes corrections start while investors are already scared of some perceived negative. Other times, they start for no apparent reason, triggering folks to seek causes-and then get scared of what they find. The volatility, on its own, can also be enough to send sentiment reeling. " Fisher Investments (emphasis added)
As founder of Templeton Funds, Sir John Templeton famously said,
Bull markets are born on pessimism, grown on skepticism, mature on optimism, and die on euphoria."
And as Fisher Investments points out, the kind of market sentiment we're seeing now doesn't correlate with the typical bear market. September 20th (the last market high) was not a time when even bears were throwing in the towel to buy stocks because "there is no alternative" or out of "fear of missing out". On September 20th we had plenty of investors worried about the same risk factors that have been with us all year. And sentiment turned bearish very quickly, not what one usually sees during an actual bear market.
That doesn't mean we might not still fall another 9% into a "baby bear market" but it does mean that such a thing is unlikely (about 18% probability based on historical data). Thus I recommend investors take advantage of this correction, buying quality undervalued stocks if you have the liquidity. If you don't (my current situation) then just sit tight and ask yourself if your emotions are reacting as you expected based on your current portfolio construction and asset allocation.
If you're losing sleep now, then you'll likely want to prepare yourself ahead of the actual bear market (likely coming about one year before the next recession) by shifting your asset allocation to one that will let you remain calm during the next economic downturn and big market slide. The average bear market lasts about 17 months and sees stocks fall 34% from all-time highs. Keep that in mind when thinking about the current 11.3% pullback from September's record high.
What 'surprise' do you see in the market that isn't currently getting sufficient investor attention? In terms of "black swans," it's impossible to know what risks might come out of left field. My personal biggest concern is China's giant debt bubble popping BUT that is something that we've been worried about for years.
Most likely 2019 will merely be dominated by the four factors I outlined previously, but obviously many factors will play into those and there will be a lot of overlap (Trade war feeds into slowing US and Global growth and yield curve inversion fears).
But I also want to point out something important which is that many of the risk factors we're worried about are self-limiting, at least to some extent. For example, the market correction is likely the reason that the Fed has suddenly done a total 180 and become more dovish. Similarly, Trump being "glued to the market" is why we got a temporary truce on trade and are now in endgame negotiations. The longer this correction lasts, and the more that current tariffs weigh on US, Chinese, and global growth, the more likely a final resolution to the trade war becomes. Meanwhile, the very same slowing growth fears that are rattling the markets now would also likely be the very thing that causes the Fed to halt rate hikes at just two more (or possibly even just one).
The Fed surprising us with just one more rate hike (and possibly cuts in 2020) and a trade deal coming sooner than expected are two huge positive catalysts that would likely end this correction and send stocks to new record highs. Combining these self-limiting risks with the still solid earnings and macro fundamentals is why I expect that 2018 will likely be a flat year for the market (0% to 5% gain). Similarly, I expect a 0% to 10% gain in 2019, depending on how the various risk factors play out.
What role will the Fed play in the coming year? In today's hypersensitive "risk off" fearful market environment, the Fed is likely going to take a dovish stance.
(Source: CNN )
Whether or not we get just one more hike, or as many as three, is going to come down to a fine balance between what stocks do over the coming weeks and months and what the macroeconomic and inflation data shows. Currently the Fed's official inflation metric, core PCE is running below its long-term 2.0% target.
(Source: Bureau of Economic Analysis)
What's more inflation pressures have been falling, not rising, debunking worries about the economy "running too hot". That gives the Fed all the reason it needs to take a measured "wait and see" approach. It usually takes 12 months for a rate hike to fully work its way through the economy and if the Fed ends up hiking even two more times (Dec and March) then we won't know the full effects on the economy until early 2020.
If the trade negotiations end up dragging on, and economic growth comes in below expectations (which are themselves trending lower) then the Fed might have to end up cutting rates to stave off a recession. That's precisely what the bond market is predicting (at least one cut in 2020). Fortunately, the Fed is run and staffed by technocrats who see the same economic data we do (and much more). As a result, the FOMC is aware that rising risks to growth might force them to reverse course soon, which means the chances of three more hikes (to the Fed's earlier estimated neutral rate of 3.0%) is looking less likely.
But that doesn't mean that the Fed is glued to the stock market ticker nearly as much as Trump is apparently. While the Fed's latest dovish reversal (both from Powell and the last Fed meeting minutes) shows that the Fed isn't going to ignore market fears, it's also not going to kowtow to short-term stock prices either. That means that anyone hoping for a James Bullard like surprise on December 19th (no rate hike at all) is likely to be disappointed.
What issue is receiving too much investor attention and/or already priced in? The thing to remember about corrections is that they are a short-term shift in sentiment. 74% of the time (on an annual basis) stocks are rising and climbing a wall of worry that includes whatever risks exist at the time. Risks are merely things that MIGHT go wrong that negatively effects fundamentals like economic and earnings growth.
During a correction sentiment shifts to the point where risks are all that investors focus on. Positive fundamentals, whether objectively good earnings results, or positive economic data, can be totally ignored, or even taken in a negative light. For example, if economic growth ends up surprising to the upside next year the market might take that as bad news because we might end up with three or even four rate more rate hikes in this tightening cycle.
But ultimately the difference between a bear market and a correction is the difference between facts and fears. Corrections are about fears of what bad things might happen, while bear markets are either triggered by crazy valuations (which we don't have) or bad things actually happening (negative economic and earnings growth).
For example, over the past 40 years, the average TTM PE for the S&P 500 has been 20.2 at a time when the average 10-year yield was 6.3%. Today the S&P 500's TTM PE is 20.0 . This means that stocks are NOT historically overvalued right now and possibly even slightly undervalued given that long-term interest rates (10-year yield) are at under 3%. For a bear market to happen means stocks have to fall about 9% more to a TTM PE of 18.2
For stocks to keep falling earnings growth expectations would have to become negative, and we're still a long way from that happening.
(Source: Factset Research)
While 2019's EPS estimates have been drifting lower from an earlier high of 10.4% they remain slightly above average (since 2002 S&P 500's CAGR EPS growth has been 7.5%). Now it's true that over the past 20 years analysts overestimate EPS growth 12 months out by 3.5% (in non-recession years). Thus we're actually likely to see about 5% earnings growth next year (2020 estimates are running about 9% so probably 5% to 6% in 2020 is more realistic).
But even modest positive growth, when combined with today's valuations and interest rate environment means that stocks are unlikely to see the kind of 50% to 65% collapse that many doomsday prophets have been warning about for years. Basically, given the actual data (the facts) I'd say the stocks are currently pricing in most of the big risks we're facing and thus likely close to bottoming.
How Are You Personally Positioning Your Portfolio For 2019 (And Beyond) (Source: Morningstar)
My portfolio is constructed to achieve strong market-beating total returns of 13% to 16% over time via three fundamental strategies.
maximum safe yield: (6.0% yield on cost, recession resistant cash flow, strong balance sheets, quality assets, and good management) strong long-term dividend growth: 14.7% five-year average dividend growth rate high margin of safety (average holding is 33% undervalued per dividend yield theory) The key to my "bunker portfolio" is that 94% of my money is invested in low-risk dividend stocks, with long-term contracted cash-flow that will hold up well in any economic, industry, or interest rate environment. And because of my rock bottom average valuation (high margin of safety), I have been experiencing far less volatility during this correction.
October: -5.75% total return vs. -6.84% for the S&P 500 November: 3.96% total return vs. 2.04% for the S&P 500 December (through Dec 14th) -3.07% vs. -5.72% for the S&P 500 October Through Mid-December: -4.62% vs. -9.66% for S&P 500 (beta 0.48) If 2019 becomes a repeat of 2018 (which it's likely to be for the first half of the year at least) then deeply undervalued, high-yield stocks including REITs (25% of my portfolio) and utilities (11%) are likely to help me outperform. I'm also 9% in healthcare, which gives me 20% defensive positioning just in case the economy tips into recession earlier than expected.
Of course, given the actual macro fundamental data and trends, we're seeing I don't expect an economic downturn to start until 2021, nor a bear market (stocks peaking) until 2020. This is why I'm also positioned in commodity insensitive and recession resistant midstream stocks (to profit from America's ongoing energy boom), technology, and economically sensitive industrials and financials.
Ultimately my approach is to always focus on the long-term fundamentals, both for the economy and my individual holdings. I ignore the market's crazy daily, weekly and month swings, and instead focus on owning quality and well-run income producing assets, that I buy at deep discounts to fair value. History has shown that this is ultimately likely to generate not just generous, safe, and fast-growing income over time, but market-beating total returns as well.
Bottom Line: The Only Certainty About 2019 Is That Stocks Will Be Predictably Unpredictable Anyone that tells you they can predict with certainty what stocks will do in the next year is either an idiot, a liar, or trying to sell you something. The truth is that the US and the global economy are massively complex organic structures made up of the decisions of billions of people, businesses, and institutions.
Meanwhile, the stock market is driven in the short-term by fickle investor sentiment, and increasingly these days, computer trading systems and passive investments like ETFs that make short-term volatility even worse. Thus the only thing I know for sure is that 2019 is going to be predictably unpredictable, with volatility likely remaining at its current levels.
The key issues for next year, which I and all investors will be watching closely are:
Fed interest rate policy (bond market pricing in just two more rate hikes including December) trade negotiations (negotiations likely to be extended beyond March and take six to 12 months) US economic growth/yield curve (10y-3m is most reliable and the one banks focus on) Slowing global growth (which is still positive and likely to remain so) Depending on how these various complex factors play out I expect the market to deliver 0% to 10% total returns next year. This potentially means stocks might be flat from 2018 through 2019. While that might seem like "market hell" to many people, in fact, it's not unusual historically speaking. The key for investors is to avoid the dangerous temptation of market timing, which history has shown is all but impossible. Rather trust your personal asset allocation to protect your wealth and achieve your long-term financial goals.
Personally, I'm not worried about my bunker retirement portfolio which, from day one, has been built with a focus on maximum safe (and recession resistant) dividends, strong long-term payout growth, and buying stocks with very high margins of safety (deeply undervalued).
Should 2019 become a repeat of 2018, a flat year marked by strong volatility and massive fear, uncertainty and doubt, I will be able to sleep very well at night. That's because, with my average holding 33% undervalued (per dividend yield theory) I have very limited downside, and with an average yield on cost of about 6.5% (for 2019) I'll earn a decent (and likely market-beating) return from safe and fast-growing dividends alone.
